passage: I'm Uma, the neighbour aunty, and I watched this from my doorstep. Tejas, who is five, got a plain red toy car in a birthday bag. Ten minutes earlier he hadn't cared about it. Then Jaya's little girl offered her shiny blue car for a swap. Tejas hugged the red one to his chest. "No! Mine is the best one!" The blue car was bigger and had working lights. He still wouldn't swap. I'm not sure what he was thinking, but he held that red car all evening.

qa.q: What did Jaya's little girl offer Tejas?
qa.a: She offered her shiny blue car for a swap.

qa.q: Why did Tejas hug the red car and call it the best one?
qa.a: Tejas felt protective of the red car once it was his, so it seemed more precious to him even though the blue car was bigger and had working lights.

qa.q: How could a grown-up help Tejas and the girl play together?
qa.a: A grown-up could suggest taking turns with both cars, so Tejas keeps his red car safe while trying the blue one.

qa.q: How might Jaya's little girl feel when Tejas refuses?
qa.a: She may feel disappointed or confused, since she offered a car with lights and got a loud no.

grounding: Shows a young boy valuing a plain toy car far more once it is his and refusing a better swap.

passage:
Monday: At the toy library, Siddharth, five, didn't even look at the wooden train. Manoj, his papa, picked it for him.
Wednesday: The train was his now. When his cousin asked to swap it for a fire truck, Siddharth shouted, "No! My train is special!" He slept with it that night.
Saturday: Time to return it. Siddharth cried. Papa said, "Take any other toy from the shelf." He shook his head hard. "I want MY train."

qa.q: Where did the wooden train come from?
qa.a: It came from the toy library.

qa.q: Why does Siddharth call the train special on Wednesday?
qa.a: Siddharth feels attached and protective once the train becomes his, so it feels precious to him even though on Monday he didn't even look at it.

qa.q: What could Papa try before the next toy-library visit?
qa.a: Papa could remind Siddharth that toys go back on Saturday and let him choose his own, so saying goodbye is expected.

qa.q: How might the cousin feel when Siddharth refuses the swap?
qa.a: The cousin may feel let down, since a fire truck seemed a fair trade for a train.

grounding: Shows a young boy who ignored a toy until it was his, then treated it as precious and refused a fair swap.

passage: The moving truck was coming at noon, and there was room for only one box of toys. Dilnaz, Bilal's mother, held up two things: his old, squashed tiger and a new puzzle that Maria from next door wanted to trade for it. "Maria will give you her puzzle for Tiger," Ammi said. Bilal, four, grabbed the tiger. "Tiger is mine! Tiger is better!" The tiger had lost an eye. Bilal didn't care. Outside, the truck honked. Tiger went in the box.

qa.q: When was the moving truck coming?
qa.a: The moving truck was coming at noon.

qa.q: Why does Bilal think Tiger is better than a new puzzle?
qa.a: Tiger is his, so it feels far more precious to him than the puzzle, even with a missing eye.

qa.q: How could Ammi make choices like this easier next time?
qa.a: Ammi could let Bilal keep his special toy and choose other things to pass on, so he doesn't feel something of his is being taken.

qa.q: How might Maria feel when Bilal refuses the trade?
qa.a: Maria may be disappointed, since a new puzzle seemed a good offer for an old tiger.

grounding: Shows a young boy valuing his worn toy far above a fair trade simply because it is his.

passage: In their Guwahati flat, Bhupen, five, clutched a small yellow rubber duck he'd won at the fair that morning. His cousin Alka held out her big shiny racing car. "Swap? Just for today?" Bhupen shook his head hard and hid the duck behind his back. "It's mine." Alka put the car down beside him. "You can have it to keep." He looked at the car. He looked at the duck. He pressed the duck to his cheek. "No. My duck." At bath time he took the duck into the bucket. The car stayed on the floor.

qa.q: Where had Bhupen won the yellow rubber duck?
qa.a: At the fair that morning.

qa.q: What does Bhupen pressing the duck to his cheek suggest he feels?
qa.a: It suggests he feels love and pride for the duck now that it is his, valuing it even more than a bigger, shinier car.

qa.q: How could Alka make a swap easier for Bhupen next time?
qa.a: She could let him play with the car while keeping his duck, instead of asking him to give up something that is his.

qa.q: How might Alka feel when Bhupen refuses even a keep-forever swap?
qa.a: Alka might be surprised or a little hurt, since she was offering her best car and he chose a small duck.

grounding: A young boy refuses to swap his new rubber duck for his cousin's bigger car, because the duck is his.

passage:
"Amandeep, look! Harleen's dinosaur roars!" said Chandrika Bua.
Amandeep, five, held his small green dinosaur from the cereal box. "Mine is better."
"Hers is bigger. It has a button. Want to swap?"
"No!"
"Just for a minute?"
"No. This is mine." He hugged it to his tummy.
Harleen pressed the button. ROAR. Amandeep's eyes went wide. He watched for a long time.
"Swap now?" Bua asked.
He shook his head. "Mine is the best one."
He put his green dinosaur on his pillow and patted it.

qa.q: Where did Amandeep's small green dinosaur come from?
qa.a: From the cereal box.

qa.q: What does Amandeep hugging the dinosaur to his tummy show about how he feels?
qa.a: It shows he feels proud and protective of the dinosaur because it is his, even though Harleen's is bigger and roars.

qa.q: What could Chandrika Bua try so that Amandeep can enjoy the roaring dinosaur?
qa.a: She could let him press the button while he keeps holding his own, so he doesn't have to give anything up.

qa.q: How might Harleen feel when Amandeep keeps saying his is better?
qa.a: Harleen might feel a bit puzzled or proud of her roaring dinosaur, and may not understand why he won't swap.

grounding: A five-year-old refuses to swap his small cereal-box dinosaur for his cousin's bigger roaring one, insisting his is best.
